paragraphs: When Zhu Xu departed Xiangyang, the city had just suffered its first frost.

The tips of the grass beyond the north gate shone white. The wagon escorting him had no cage; old felt covered its boards, and until they reached Nanyang he was allowed to step down and walk at the relay stations, though never out of the guards’ sight. Qin soldiers had taken his sword but permitted him to carry his old clothes and a box of books. As he was about to pass through the gate, a soldier who had defended the city beside him saluted from a distance. Zhu Xu raised his hand in return. The man’s eyes reddened. He ducked into an alley and did not look back.

Passing through the gate tunnel, Zhu Xu remembered the sharp crack of the rope breaking as the drawbridge fell on the night the city was taken. The crossbars had since been replaced. The ruts of carts that had passed half a month ago remained in the mud beside the road. Qin soldiers were repairing a wall breached by a stone projectile; among those carrying bricks were Xiangyang craftsmen and infantrymen in the short coats of Qin. Across the rim of a well a woman argued with a military clerk over compensation for her collapsed house. Her shouting had stopped several men at their work.
Zhu Xu had intended not to look. In the end he turned his head.
“Will they pay her?” he asked the officer riding beside the wagon.
“Her claim goes into the register first. The sum must still be verified.”
“If it takes until next year to verify, where will she sleep meanwhile?”
The officer was silent for a moment, then asked one of his riders to note the ward’s name. Such a small act might change nothing. Zhu Xu remembered the officer’s face all the same.

Outside Nanyang lay a field of new graves, each marked with a short wooden tablet of the same size, though some names had been cut deeper than others. In the wind the tablets swayed together, like soldiers still waiting to be called to roll. Zhu Xu asked the wagon to stop. The officer did not ask why. He merely had his men give the prisoner room.
“Were they killed attacking Xiangyang?”
“About half. Others guarded the grain road or drowned crossing the Han. Some were carried back from beneath the walls and died of fever afterward.”

Zhu Xu went closer. Each board bore a unit number, a name, and the soldier’s home district. Beside some lay small tokens of home custom: a lock of horsehair, a worn knot of hemp, half a coin rubbed white. No one had added the titles of vanished kingdoms before these names. Neither had anyone struck out the villages from which the men had come.
“Did they serve in the same squads?”
“Some did. Where they are buried together, the places follow the squad rolls. Their families can find them more easily that way.”

Zhu Xu crouched and set a fallen grave marker upright in the earth. The officer waited quietly. He understood that the captured commander might be remembering another roll of names, those who had died beneath the walls of Xiangyang on the other side.

The officer was Lu Guang, a man of Hedong serving as a staff major in Central Army headquarters. At the Yu River relay post, Zhu Xu saw a grain official publicly berating a carter. The cart had arrived half a day late, he claimed, and the army would be short a full wagon of fodder. The driver dared not answer back. He begged only to be allowed to seat his old mother in the empty cart and carry her as far as the village entrance. The official raised his whip high, but before it fell Lu Guang stepped forward and pulled a warrant from his sleeve.
“The time of requisition is written here. The driver is not late. You took an extra watch to inspect the cart at the station, then blamed the man for it.”

Seeing the Central Army officer, the grain official quickly lowered his whip, though he continued muttering about the ruined road. Lu ordered the overdue grain allowance added to the driver’s account for verification at headquarters. Once the crowd dispersed, Zhu Xu remarked, “Your laws make fine reading. What if you had not happened past today?”
Lu looked at the whip mark in the mud. He walked a few paces before answering. “Then one can only hope the carter can read, and knows how to take his warrant and make a complaint.”
“And if he cannot read?”
“Find someone who can. If he finds no one, he suffers the loss.”

It was not a pleasing answer. Zhu Xu found it more credible than the courtly speeches that praised an age of perfect justice. A few miles later he asked Lu Guang, “You are Han. Why are you content to lead soldiers for the Fu clan?”

Lu looked at the wheel turning before them. The axle was making an ugly sound; he put out his hand to steady it. “When I wandered in the west as a young man, it was a Qin soldier who gave me my first bowl of army grain. Later, in battle, a Xianbei man saved me in the front rank and a Di man helped bury my father. Which one am I supposed to choose to hate?”
“Jin was your former dynasty.”
“You defend Jin, Governor, and I imagine it is not merely because the Jin court gave you office. I have my own reasons for serving in Qin, and my own difficulties.”
Zhu Xu had intended to argue further. At the word “difficulties,” he closed his mouth.

By the time they entered the passes, autumn rain had turned to wet snow. A decree from Chang’an ordered that Zhu Xu wear no shackles and be paraded before no crowd of captives. He was to stay in the separate residence of the Court for State Guests, forbidden to travel beyond the checkpoints or exchange private military letters with the southern court. Only after three gates had inspected their documents did the wagon enter the capital. Charcoal sellers were shouting their wares in the street; children chased a scrawny dog beneath the eaves. Through a gap in the curtain Zhu Xu saw clothing of every kind. Xianbei traders bargained in halting Chinese, while the distant sound of a foreign reed pipe floated beyond a ward wall. For a moment he could not tell whose old capital this was meant to be.

He spent three days at the Court for State Guests. Clerks brought millet and charcoal at regular hours, and even a pot of old tea from Xiangyang. He kept the tea but did not drink it. An old bronze inkstone remained on his desk. On the third morning a palace messenger asked whether he wished to change his clothes before the audience. Zhu Xu put on the deep-robed garment once bestowed upon him by Jin. At his waist was the leather belt from which his sword had been taken, still empty.

No banquet had been arranged in Chengming Hall. On Fu Jian’s table lay only a map of the Jiang-Han river region and two rolls of household registers compiled after the siege. Fu Rong sat at the side; behind the desk Fu Hong held his brush ready. Zhu Xu entered and bowed with folded hands. “Zhu Xu, who served Jin as defender of Xiangyang, greets the King of Qin.”
“Offer him a seat,” Fu Jian said.
Zhu Xu remained standing. “As a defeated commander, I dare not sit among Qin ministers.”
Fu Jian instructed a chamberlain to bring a separate guest seat below the dais. “Since you still call yourself a Jin official, you shall be received as a guest. Was the journey cold?”
“Snow comes earlier in the north than in Xiangyang.”
“Did you travel safely?”
“I passed graves belonging to your army. I also saw an official with a whip requisitioning grain.”
Fu Jian set down his brush. “Where?”

Zhu Xu described the post near the Yu River and the carter, and how Lu Guang had examined the warrant. He gave the details without embellishment. Fu Hong recorded them one by one and asked the official’s name. Zhu Xu did not know it; he remembered only that one black button was missing from the man’s collar.
“With the place known, we can investigate,” Fu Hong said.

Zhu Xu studied the Crown Prince. He was young, with a faint scar on his right cheek, and the hand that held the brush did not move easily. Zhu Xu did not know the injury had come from the fighting at Wei Bridge. The young man looked more like a recorder in a field headquarters than an heir waiting to hear crowds cry long life to him.
Fu Jian spread out the map. “I wish to ask about places beyond Xiangyang.”
Zhu Xu straightened slightly.
“Where does the Jiangling fleet winter? How many commands of Huan Chong’s old army remain? Which troops has Jiankang lately moved toward the Huai?”
Zhu Xu heard all three questions and answered each with the same words: “I do not know.”
“You have served many years in Jing and Xiang,” Fu Jian said. “You know none of these things?”
“I know part of them.”
“Then why will you not say?”
“Having failed to hold Xiangyang, I will not purchase my own life by handing over more Jin soldiers to the Qin court.”
A young attendant official could not contain himself. “The Heavenly King lets you wear your own robes and seats you as a guest. Is this how you answer him?”
Zhu Xu looked at the man. “If you were defeated today, would you explain Qin’s grain roads to the government in Jiankang?”

The official flushed and was ready to step forward, but Fu Jian raised a hand to stop him. He did not immediately change the subject. Moving his finger across the map to Xiangyang, he asked, “Li Bohu opened the gate to us. Do you hate him?”
“Yes.”
“He saved many of the townspeople.”
“I know that too.”
“You know, and yet you hate him?”
“If I said I did not hate him, he would become a loyal officer in my eyes. What then of the men who fought and bled for months to defend Xiangyang?”
Fu Jian was quiet a moment, then nodded. “I understand that.”

He ordered the military map put away and the fire replenished. Outside, snow began falling again, quickly dusting the palace tiles white. Zhu Xu thought the audience was ending, but Fu Jian suddenly said, “Some in Chang’an urge me to press our advantage and take Jiangling. How would the people of the south respond?”
“Does the King of Qin wish to hear praise?” Zhu Xu asked.
“If I did, there are plenty of men outside who would write it.”

Zhu Xu considered a moment. Rising from the guest seat, he crossed to a roll of postwar Xiangyang registers. He opened it to a family of three who had fled through the south gate. The father had died on the journey; wife and child remained in Nanyang awaiting settlement. The clerk had recorded two dou of millet issued to them, but no place where they might live.

“If this family finds a decent life, then the next time it hears Qin troops are coming it may not be as frightened as when the siege began. But if in another year they still cannot rent a patch of land, they may say they would rather have died in Xiangyang.”
Fu Jian asked, “Not everyone in the south loves Jin. Why, then, do they help its soldiers?”

Zhu Xu smoothed the page. “When I requisitioned grain in Xiangyang, the people cursed me. When the war drums sounded beneath the walls, they helped carry stones. Some who had cursed me died before my eyes.”
“For the house of Jin?”

“Some of them. Others feared their homes would burn, their ancestors’ graves would be disturbed, their children taken as slaves. Men standing upon the same wall need not be thinking of the same thing.”
Fu Rong asked, “And if Qin truly neither takes their land nor moves them by force?”
“Will what Qin promises today still hold next year? If one frontier city keeps its soldiers disciplined, can every office along the grain road be trusted to do the same?”

Fu Rong remembered the unregistered military households discovered after the fighting at Wei Bridge. He did not answer. Fu Jian stepped down from the dais and closed the household roll with his own hands.
“I did not loose my soldiers upon Xiangyang after the city fell.”
“I know.”
“I ordered houses repaired and grain distributed.”
“If those houses are truly repaired, the people who live in them will remember.”
“Yet they still call themselves Jin people.”
“Your Majesty,” Zhu Xu said, “their families have lived in that city for generations. Yours have been there only a few months.”

Fu Jian sighed softly. He was older than Zhu Xu. He knew a man’s lifetime was short, while the habits of a city endured beyond reckoning. Yet how could he willingly leave a hundred years to others, when he had spent his own days marching from Guanzhong to conquer Yan, take Shu, and subdue Liang? He left these thoughts unspoken and asked instead, “Now that you are in Chang’an, will you accept an office under Qin?”
“No.”
“What of a position as an advisory gentleman? You need not attend court or discuss Jin military affairs, only help the finance offices settle the households formerly belonging to Xiangyang.”
“That would still mean accepting a Qin seal and ribbon.”
“What if I ask only that you examine the cases, without taking a seal?”

Zhu Xu looked again at the unfinished household register. Still he shook his head. “I can tell Your Highness about a carter struck with a whip. I cannot decide for Qin how much grain a province should levy. Give it time, and no one would remember the difference.”

Fu Jian did not press him. Turning to Fu Hong, he said, “Prepare a warrant for a resident guest. Zhu Xu shall continue to be styled former defender of Xiangyang. He may not leave the capital or send private military letters. The Court for State Guests will provide his lodging and necessities. Seal away the appointment to the advisory office for now; we can ask him again another day. If he has observations concerning civilian affairs, he may submit them.”
Zhu Xu remained silent a long while before bowing. “The King of Qin has allowed me to keep this remnant of my former name. I am grateful.”
“You still refuse to call yourself my subject?”
“I do.”
Fu Jian laughed, though weariness touched the smile. “Then so be it.”
As he was leaving, Zhu Xu stopped at the door. “Once the registers of those who left the city have been verified, may I see a copy?”
“Those parts unrelated to the army may be shown you,” Fu Hong replied. “If you know any of the missing families, please add their names.”
Zhu Xu nodded. It was perhaps the one request he had not intended to make that day.
Two days later, the Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Yao Chang, heard of the audience and asked an official at the Court for State Guests, “Does Governor Zhu still wear his old robes?”
“He does.”
“Has he drunk the tea?”
“He has not.”

Yao smiled and instructed them to send no more official gifts. A few days later a merchant appeared at Zhu Xu’s door with a box of southern tea cakes and an old-style brush and inkstone. If the governor wished to write home, the man said, he could carry letters along merchant routes that reached both Jiangling and Jiankang.

Zhu Xu had the merchant wait in the porch and came out to meet him. The man claimed that his wife and children lived in Luoyang and that he had once sold paper in Xiangyang. As if in passing, Zhu Xu asked during which season rice prices had begun to rise there the previous year. The visitor gave the wrong month. Zhu Xu pushed the tea chest back toward him.
“Who sent you?”
“No one. I came out of respect for you.”
“If I wrote in a letter that Qin intended a southern campaign, would you carry that too?”
Something flashed in the merchant’s eyes. “What does Your Excellency know?”
“I know nothing,” Zhu Xu said. “If you were truly a merchant, you would not have asked that question first.”

The man had nothing to say. He claimed only that Lord Yao respected loyalty, and had meant no harm. Zhu Xu told him to repeat those words exactly to whoever had sent him, and to add one more message: “My letters to my family in Jin need no messenger outside the official post. If your routes are good enough to evade the checkpoints, a single letter could cost many people their lives.”

The merchant departed with his box. Zhu Xu did not make an accusation. He had only a few suspicious words, and no witness who could prove Yao Chang had ordered anything. Instead, he copied out the description recorded by his doorkeeper, the route the merchant had named, and the shop mark cut into the wrapper around the tea cakes. He folded the sheet and placed it inside his book chest. As a captured commander, he knew there were things best left unsaid until one could be certain of them.

As the spring cold eased, Zhu Xu was sometimes allowed to leave his ward. Passing through the western market, he saw a Han craftsman quarrel with a Xianbei soldier over the price of horse harness. A Qiang soldier joined in, speaking the dialect of Guanzhong. By the end of the quarrel all three were drinking from the same bowl of water. Farther on, a patrol found its way blocked by a charcoal cart sunk into a mud hole. Their commander ordered four men to dismount and lift the wheel. Two slipped as they heaved and fell together, cursing and laughing. Zhu Xu watched from the roadside for a long while.

His thoughts still returned to Jiangling and Jiankang, to the men in the southern court who had treated him as one of their own. He knew that if a way home ever opened, he would defend Jin again. Yet he could no longer speak of this northern capital merely with the word “barbarians” he had heard in childhood. It had cruel officials, deserters, and merchants carrying secret messages. In its streets people waited for missing kin. The Xianbei soldier who helped lift a charcoal cart today might only yesterday have been fighting a Di soldier in Beidi. If Fu Jian could keep such people living in one city for long enough, then the southerners would one day face a power in the north unlike any they had known.

The evening sun slanted above the ward wall. Zhu Xu touched the empty sword belt at his waist and turned back toward the Court for State Guests. On the table lay a new household register from Xiangyang, several families newly added at the end in the column for those seeking relatives. He ground his ink, spread a sheet of paper, and filled in the surnames he recognized, one by one.
When the city fell, Zhu Xu lost Xiangyang. In Chang’an, there were still some names he would not let go.
